title: Porous contents, salvage and contamination
audience: Coordinators, supervisors and trained workers who may be asked about, triage, refer or document cleaning and water-removal work after a flood or water event. Not a qualification or authority to enter a flood-affected building, energise its systems, or certify it as dry, safe or habitable.
learningOutcomes: Recognise that porous contents may hold contamination that a wipe-down does not remove, and route salvage decisions to authorised assessment.

instruction.heading: Scope and authority
instruction.body: This lesson teaches how porous contents are quarantined, and how each salvage decision is linked to evidence, consent and an authorised assessor. It does not restore, clean or dispose of porous items on the basis of a wipe-down. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instruction.heading: Porous contents, salvage and contamination
instruction.body: Porous furnishings, insulation and wallboard may keep contamination that cannot be seen on the surface, so a visual wipe-down is not sufficient evidence of restoration. Quarantine the items and defer any decision to restore or dispose of them to an authorised, competent assessment. Prepare a chain-of-decision record that links the identity of each item, the contamination concern, the owner's consent and the authority for its disposition. Keep the record so that any later decision can be traced back to the evidence.

procedure: Quarantine porous items such as furnishings, insulation and wallboard, and label each one.
Record the identity and location of each item with photographs.
Record the contamination concern, its source and the time since the intrusion.
Obtain the owner's consent and record it.
Refer the restore or dispose decision to an authorised, competent assessor.
Keep the chain-of-decision record, so that each decision can be traced to its evidence.

workedExamples.situation: A wet sofa and insulation are wiped down, and the crew says they are now restored.
workedExamples.reasoning: No. A visual wipe-down does not show that porous contents are free of contamination. Quarantine the items and refer the decision to an authorised assessor.

workedExamples.situation: A carpet looks dry after a wipe, and the owner wants it reinstalled today.
workedExamples.reasoning: Hold the reinstallation. Record the carpet, the concern and the owner's request, and refer the decision.

equipmentAndPpe: Gloves and bags for quarantined items, selected from the hazard assessment.

commonErrors.error: Relying on a wipe-down to show that porous contents are restored.
commonErrors.prevention: Quarantine porous items and refer the decision.

commonErrors.error: Disposing of an item without the owner's consent and a record.
commonErrors.prevention: Record consent and the authority for disposal before any disposal.

commonErrors.error: Reinstalling porous material that has not been assessed.
commonErrors.prevention: Hold reinstallation until the assessor has decided.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This lesson does not authorise restoration, cleaning or disposal of porous items. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.
Porous furnishings, insulation and wallboard can keep contamination that cannot be seen on the surface.

qualityStandard: The learner quarantines porous items and does not accept a wipe-down as restoration.
The learner links each decision to the owner's consent and the authority for it.
documentationEvidence: Chain-of-decision record: item, concern, owner consent, authority for disposition.

knowledgeChecks.question: A wet sofa and insulation are cleaned with a wipe-down. Is the wipe-down enough to show that the items are restored?
options: Yes, because the surface looks clean and the items have been wiped down by the crew this morning
Yes, if the owner agrees to accept the items as they are, since they look fine to them and they want them back
No. Porous items can keep contamination not visible on the surface. Quarantine them and refer the decision.

knowledgeChecks.question: What must a chain-of-decision record link?
options: Item identity, the contamination concern, the owner's consent and the authority for its disposition

moduleAuthority.heading: Module authority and restricted work
moduleAuthority.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to enter a flood-affected building, to carry out regulated flood restoration, to energise or isolate electrical, gas or solar systems, to remove sewage or contaminated water, to dispose of waste, or to certify that a property is dry, hygienic, structurally sound or safe to occupy. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate or approval. Some of the work described is restricted to licensed, authorised or specially trained people, including electrical and gas work, structural assessment, sewage handling and some disposal. The site controller, the owner, the insurer and the competent professionals each hold separate decisions, and none of them replaces the others. Where the controlling authority or the competent professional is not identified, stop and refer.

stopWorkAndReferral.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
stopWorkAndReferral.body: Stop and refer whenever any of these is true: permission to enter or written safety clearance is missing; the contamination is unknown; a structural hazard, a slip or a confined space has not been cleared; an electrical, gas or solar system is water-exposed or has not been licensed for re-energisation; an exposure has occurred or controls are not in place; the equipment or operators are not suitable; porous material is in question; hidden microbial contamination is suspected; a waste route is not yet known; or a party asks for a dry, hygienic or occupancy statement. A stop-work decision is correct. Record it, and restart only after the competent party has confirmed the scope in writing.
